source_text: Ut conditionem suam conditione sua perdat, et sit absque hoc, sine quo non posse esse definitum est. Hoc est inficiari rebus. Quid tale Anaxagoras, qui nivem nigram esse dicebat? Commentaris rei alicuius naturam suis fructibus negari; cumque sit contrarium necessitas et voluntas, ita ut, sicut supra ostendimus, mutua se impugnatione consumant; tu novo impossibilique foedere ac necessitudine monstruosa alterum alterius subdis effectui, et dicis necessitatem de fructibus voluntatis exortam, ut voluntas sua se multiplicatione deleverit, et statum proprium operata mutaverit; atque, ut rem ipsam suis vocabulis exprimamus, postquam coepit voluntas esse, voluntas esse desierit. Quo quid potest, non dico obtusius, sed furiosius cogitari? Cum ergo haec duo simul esse non possint, id est, necessitas et voluntas, tuque confirmaveris quod diximus, non posse esse sine voluntate delictum, assentiaris quo ⁄ que non esse in parvulis voluntatem; contorto gutture cogeris annuere nullum in his esse peccatum quod sine voluntate non posse esse professus es.
pass_a_gloss: That it may lose its condition by its condition, and be without that without which it has been defined that it cannot be. This is to disown the things. What of such a kind did Anaxagoras, who said snow is black? You invent that the nature of some thing is denied by its fruits; and since necessity and will are contrary, so that, as we showed above, they consume each other by mutual attack; you by a new and impossible treaty and a monstrous necessity subjoin one to the effect of the other, and you say that necessity arose from the fruits of will, so that will destroyed itself by its own multiplication, and having worked changed its own status; and, that we may express the thing itself by its own words, after will began to be, will ceased to be. Than which what can be thought, I do not say more dull, but more furious? Since therefore these two cannot be together, that is, necessity and will, and you have confirmed what we said, that there cannot be offense without will, and you also assent that there is not will in little ones; with a twisted throat you are compelled to grant that there is no sin in them which you have professed cannot be without will.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice

LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Thus it is to lose its own condition through its own condition, and exist without what it was defined as unable to exist without! This is denying reality. What comparable thing did Anaxagoras do when he said snow was black? You invent the claim that a thing’s nature is denied by its own fruits. Necessity and will are opposites, so that, as I showed above, they destroy one another by mutual conflict. Yet through a new and impossible alliance and a monstrous relationship, you make one arise as the other’s effect. You say necessity grew from the fruits of will, so that will erased itself by multiplying itself and changed its own condition through its activity. To state the matter in its own terms: after will began to be will, it ceased to be will. What could be imagined, I will not say more stupid, but more insane? Since these two, necessity and will, cannot coexist, and since you have confirmed my statement that an offense cannot exist without will, while also agreeing that infants have no will, you are dragged by the throat into admitting that there is no sin in them, since you professed that sin cannot exist without will.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
